newsitem.title: INDIA: India warns over subsidies worth 14 percent of GDP.
newsitem.headline: India warns over subsidies worth 14 percent of GDP.

text.p: India's Finance Ministry said on Tuesday it paid out subsidies worth more than 14 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1994-95 and warned unjustified payouts were adding to the country's deficit and interest rates.

"The aggregate level of subsidy in 1994-95 for all services provided by the central and state governments is placed at 1,373.38 billion rupees and constituted 14.4 percent of GDP," the ministry said in a report sent to parliament.

The ministry, which urged reform of the subsidy system, said: "The macroeconomic costs of unjustified subsidies are mirrored in persistent large fiscal deficit and, consequently, higher interest rates."
The ministry classifies subsidies according to two categories -- "merit" and "non-merit" goods.

Merit goods and services include primary education, public health, sewerage and sanitation, social welfare schemes, roads and bridges, flood control and drainage, agriculture research and various scientific research programmes.
The remaining goods and services are labelled "non-merit" goods.
The case for subsidising merit goods was the strongest, the ministry said, but subsidies on non-merit goods in the 1994/95 fiscal year ending March were estimated at 10.7 of GDP.
"Some of the known subsidies like food, fertiliser and education beyond primary level, are not counted in the group of merit services."
It said subsidies were not properly targeted at the poor and there was widespread leakage.

It suggested that reform should focus on cuts in subsidies and greater transparency. Subsidies should be paid for a specified time, used for strict economic objectives and given to final products alone.
The key to reducing subsidies was a phased increase in user charges, the ministry said, adding there was scope for raising prices in irrigation, power, transport, agriculture and industry.
"Recovery rates, even for non-merit services, are very low. An increase in user charges would substantially mitigate pressures on (the) fiscal deficit," the report said.
The subsidy rate, which measures the subsidy incurred net of recovery, for non-merit services stood at 90 percent.
The ministry said it was possible to target slashing the non-merit goods' subsidy rate to 50 percent in three years, and to aim to reduce it to 25 percent in another two years.
Cutting the subsidy rate to 50 percent would reduce the combined fiscal deficit of the federal and state governments, which stood at 6.5 percent of GDP in 1996/97, to less than 2.0 percent, it said.
